intro: Apple hires machine learning engineers into product teams rather than a central research org, so the loop is run by the team and tests whether you can ship models that work on a billion devices: accurate, small, fast, private, and debuggable. Expect fewer trick algorithm puzzles than at Google and more depth on fundamentals, on-device constraints, your own past work, and clean implementation.

areas.name: Siri and Apple Intelligence (AIML)
areas.focus: ASR, NLU and intent classification, on-device and server foundation models, retrieval, safety and evaluation of generative features.

areas.name: Camera, Photos and Vision
areas.focus: Image classification and segmentation, computational photography, face and scene understanding, on-device inference in the Neural Engine.

areas.name: Health, Fitness and Sensors
areas.focus: Time-series models on accelerometer, heart-rate and ECG signals, anomaly detection, clinical-grade validation, extreme battery constraints.

areas.name: Maps, Search and Recommendations
areas.focus: Ranking and retrieval, embeddings, query understanding, App Store and Music recommendations, A/B testing at scale.

areas.name: Platform and Core ML
areas.focus: Model compression, quantization, compiler and runtime work, Core ML tooling, benchmarks across Apple silicon.

process.what: Background, team match, visa and timeline. Ask which team and what the loop looks like for that team: coding only, or coding plus ML depth plus design.
process.prep: Have a two-minute summary of your best ML project with the metric you moved and the trade-off you made.

process.what: One engineer. Usually one coding problem (arrays, strings, hash maps, sometimes a small ML routine such as k-nearest neighbours or a metric) and 15-20 minutes of ML questions tied to your resume.
process.prep: Solve the Apple track Easy and Medium problems until they are automatic; rehearse explaining bias-variance, regularization and evaluation metrics without notes.

process.stage: Take-home or ML coding round (team dependent)
process.what: Some teams send a small dataset and ask for a model, a notebook, and a write-up; others do a live 'implement X from scratch' round (softmax, attention, k-means, a metric).
process.prep: Practise the ML Coding problems in this bank with a timer. For take-homes, spend as much time on the write-up (data checks, baseline, error analysis, next steps) as on the model.

process.what: Typically: 1-2 coding rounds, 1 ML fundamentals round (derivations, trade-offs, 'what would you do if'), 1 ML system design round, 1 past-work deep dive, and a hiring-manager or team-fit conversation. Senior roles add a research or architecture discussion.
process.prep: Each interviewer writes an independent assessment; the hiring manager decides. Consistency matters: a weak fundamentals round is rarely saved by a strong coding round.

process.what: An interviewer picks one project from your resume and goes as deep as you let them: data, labels, features, model choice, training setup, metrics, failures, what shipped, what you would redo.
process.prep: Prepare two projects to this depth. Bring numbers. Be able to draw the pipeline and name the hardest bug.

process.what: Collaboration with hardware, design and privacy teams; handling ambiguity; disagreement with a lead; shipping under secrecy. Apple weighs team fit heavily because the team makes the call.
process.prep: Six STAR stories: a model that failed in production, a disagreement you lost gracefully, a privacy or ethics constraint you designed around, a deadline trade-off, mentoring, and a cross-functional win.

topics.name: ML fundamentals
topics.why: The fundamentals round is where most Apple MLE loops are decided. Interviewers probe until you reach the edge of what you know, so depth beats breadth.
study: Bias-variance decomposition and how regularization, data size, model capacity and ensembling move each term.
Loss functions and what they assume: MSE (Gaussian noise), MAE, Huber, cross-entropy (multinomial), hinge, focal loss for imbalance.
Regularization: L1 vs L2 geometry, dropout as ensembling, early stopping, data augmentation, weight decay vs L2 under Adam.
Evaluation: precision/recall/F1, ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC under imbalance, calibration (ECE, reliability diagrams), threshold selection from a business cost.
Validation: stratified and grouped k-fold, time-series splits, leakage (target, temporal, duplicate), why the test set is touched once.
Optimization: SGD with momentum, Adam and AdamW, learning-rate schedules and warm-up, gradient clipping, why batch size interacts with learning rate.
Feature handling: scaling, one-hot vs target encoding vs embeddings, missing values, high-cardinality categoricals, leakage through encoders.
must_know: Derive the gradient of logistic regression with cross-entropy.
Explain why accuracy is misleading at 1% positive rate and what you report instead.
State the bias-variance trade-off in one sentence and give one lever for each side.

topics.name: Classical ML
topics.why: Many Apple product models are still gradient-boosted trees or linear models on carefully engineered features because they are small, fast and interpretable on device.
study: Linear and logistic regression, closed-form vs gradient methods, multicollinearity, interpretation of coefficients.
Decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM): split criteria, depth vs number of trees, learning rate, handling of missing values and categoricals.
SVMs and the kernel trick at a conceptual level; when a kernel method is a bad idea (n large).
k-NN, k-means, GMMs and EM, hierarchical clustering, choosing k (elbow, silhouette), the curse of dimensionality.
PCA (eigen decomposition of covariance, explained variance, whitening), t-SNE and UMAP as visualization only.
Naive Bayes and why it works despite the independence assumption.
must_know: Compare GBDT with a neural net for tabular data: when each wins and why.
Explain EM for a two-component Gaussian mixture.
Explain why PCA before k-means can help.

topics.name: Deep learning
topics.why: Vision, speech and language teams expect you to reason about architectures at the level of tensor shapes, memory and FLOPs, not just names.
study: Backpropagation by hand for a two-layer MLP; vanishing and exploding gradients; initialization (Xavier, He).
Normalization: batch norm (train vs inference, why it hurts with small batches), layer norm, group norm, RMSNorm.
CNNs: receptive field, strided vs dilated conv, depthwise separable conv (MobileNet) and why it matters on device, residual connections.
Sequence models: RNN/LSTM/GRU gating, then transformers: self-attention, multi-head, positional encodings (absolute, rotary), masking, KV cache, O(n^2) memory.
Training at scale: mixed precision, gradient accumulation, data vs model parallelism, checkpointing, reproducibility.
Transfer learning and fine-tuning: linear probe vs full fine-tune vs LoRA/adapters, catastrophic forgetting, when to freeze.
Self-supervised learning at a conceptual level: contrastive (SimCLR, CLIP), masked modelling (BERT, MAE).
must_know: Write scaled dot-product attention from scratch, with the causal mask.
Count parameters and FLOPs of a conv layer and of an attention layer.
Explain what batch norm does at inference time.

topics.name: NLP and LLMs
topics.why: Apple Intelligence put foundation models on device and on Private Cloud Compute. Teams across Siri, Messages and Mail now ask about LLM fine-tuning, evaluation and safety.
study: Tokenization (BPE, SentencePiece), embeddings, subword trade-offs for multilingual input.
Decoder-only vs encoder-only vs encoder-decoder; what each is good for.
Fine-tuning stack: SFT, preference optimization (RLHF with PPO, DPO), instruction data quality, reward hacking.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: LoRA, adapters per feature (Apple ships many small adapters on one base model).
Retrieval-augmented generation: chunking, embedding models, hybrid search, re-ranking, evaluation of groundedness.
Decoding: greedy, beam, top-k, nucleus, temperature; speculative decoding for latency.
Evaluation of generative systems: human preference, LLM-as-judge pitfalls, task-specific metrics, hallucination and safety red-teaming.
must_know: Explain LoRA in two sentences and its memory saving.
Explain why perplexity is not enough to evaluate an assistant.
Describe how a KV cache changes decoding cost.

topics.name: On-device ML and efficiency
topics.why: This is the most Apple-specific area. Almost every team cares about latency, memory, battery and the Neural Engine, and interviewers will push on it even for server roles.
study: Quantization: post-training (int8, 4-bit weight-only), quantization-aware training, per-channel vs per-tensor scales, outlier channels, what breaks (softmax, layer norm).
Pruning (unstructured vs structured), knowledge distillation (soft targets, temperature), low-rank factorization, palettization (weight clustering, which Apple's Core ML tools expose).
Architecture choices for mobile: depthwise separable convs, MobileNet/EfficientNet-style scaling, small transformers, early-exit.
The inference stack: Core ML model format, compute units (CPU, GPU, Neural Engine), operator support, memory-mapped weights, why some ops fall back to CPU.
Measuring: p50/p99 latency, peak memory, energy per inference, thermal throttling; benchmarking on the oldest supported device.
Model updates: on-device personalization, versioning models with the app, A/B testing when telemetry is limited.
must_know: Estimate memory of a 3B-parameter model at fp16, int8 and 4-bit.
Explain distillation and when it beats quantization.
Explain what a model does that would run on the GPU instead of the Neural Engine.

topics.name: Privacy-preserving ML
topics.why: Privacy is a product feature at Apple. Expect at least one question about training or evaluating without seeing raw user data.
study: Differential privacy: epsilon, the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, local vs central DP, privacy budgets; Apple uses local DP for usage statistics.
Federated learning: FedAvg, client sampling, secure aggregation, non-IID data, communication cost, and its combination with DP.
Private Cloud Compute at a conceptual level: stateless processing, verifiable software, no data retention.
On-device training and personalization, synthetic data, and how to evaluate a model you cannot inspect user inputs for.
must_know: Define epsilon-differential privacy in one sentence and give the intuition.
Describe FedAvg and its two biggest practical problems.

topics.name: Statistics and experimentation
topics.why: Ranking and product teams ask about A/B tests and estimation; health teams ask about validation and uncertainty.
study: Hypothesis testing, p-values, confidence intervals, power and sample-size, multiple comparisons.
A/B testing: randomization units, novelty effects, variance reduction (CUPED), guardrail metrics, interference.
Bayes' rule and conditional probability, common distributions, maximum likelihood vs MAP, the bootstrap.
Uncertainty in predictions: calibration, conformal prediction, when to abstain.
must_know: Compute the sample size for detecting a 1% lift at 80% power, at least by stating the formula.
Explain the difference between a confidence interval and a credible interval.

topics.name: ML system design and MLOps
topics.why: The design round is 45 minutes on a product problem end to end: data, labels, features, model, serving, monitoring, iteration.
study: A reusable template: clarify the product goal and constraints, define the metric (offline and online), data and labelling, features, baseline then model, training pipeline, serving (on device vs server), monitoring and retraining, failure modes.
Retrieval-then-ranking architectures, two-tower models, approximate nearest neighbour search, feature stores, embeddings freshness.
Data pipelines: label quality, annotation guidelines, active learning, dataset versioning, drift detection.
Serving: batching, caching, model registry, shadow and canary deployments, rollbacks.
Monitoring: input drift, prediction drift, delayed labels, slice-based evaluation, alerting thresholds.
must_know: Walk through the template in under three minutes on any product problem.
Explain how you would evaluate a model before and after shipping when labels arrive weeks later.

questions.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off and give one concrete lever for each side.
questions.a: Expected test error decomposes into irreducible noise, bias squared (error from a model too simple to capture the signal) and variance (sensitivity to the particular training sample). Lowering bias: a bigger model, more features, less regularization, training longer. Lowering variance: more data, regularization, ensembling/bagging, early stopping, dropout. Modern deep nets complicate the picture (double descent), but the vocabulary is still how interviewers expect you to diagnose under- vs over-fitting from train and validation curves.

questions.q: Derive the gradient of logistic regression with cross-entropy loss.
questions.a: With p = sigmoid(w.x + b) and loss L = -[y log p + (1-y) log(1-p)], the chain rule gives dL/dz = p - y where z = w.x + b, because dL/dp = (p-y)/(p(1-p)) and dp/dz = p(1-p). So dL/dw = (p - y) x and dL/db = p - y, averaged over the batch. The 'prediction minus label' form is the same one you get for softmax with cross-entropy and for linear regression with MSE, which is a good follow-up to mention.

questions.q: Your classifier has 99% accuracy on a dataset with 1% positives. What do you report instead?
questions.a: Accuracy equals the majority-class rate, so it says nothing. Report precision, recall and F1 at the operating threshold, the PR curve and PR-AUC (ROC-AUC is optimistic under heavy imbalance because false-positive rate stays small), and the confusion matrix with the business cost of each cell. Then choose the threshold from that cost, not from 0.5. During training consider class weights, focal loss or resampling, and make sure the validation split keeps the real prevalence.

questions.q: L1 vs L2 regularization: what is the difference in effect and why?
questions.a: Both shrink weights, but L1 (lasso) drives some weights exactly to zero and so performs feature selection, while L2 (ridge) shrinks all weights smoothly. Geometrically, the L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners sit on the axes, so the loss contours tend to touch it at a point where some coordinates are zero; the L2 ball is round and touches anywhere. In the Bayesian view L1 is a Laplace prior and L2 a Gaussian prior on the weights. With Adam, L2 in the loss and decoupled weight decay (AdamW) are not equivalent, which is why AdamW is the default now.

questions.q: What is data leakage? Give three ways it sneaks in.
questions.a: Leakage is any information in training that will not be available at prediction time, which inflates offline metrics. Common sources: target leakage through features derived from the label (e.g. 'refund issued' when predicting fraud); temporal leakage when random splits put future rows in training; preprocessing fitted on the full dataset (scalers, target encoders, vocabulary) before the split; duplicates or near-duplicates across splits; and group leakage when the same user appears in both splits. The defence is to split first, fit everything inside the training fold, and split by time or by group when that matches deployment.

questions.q: How do you pick a decision threshold for a binary classifier?
questions.a: From the cost of each outcome, not from 0.5. Compute precision and recall (or expected cost) across thresholds on validation data with the deployment prevalence, then choose the threshold that meets the product constraint: a fixed precision floor for a user-facing feature, a recall floor for a safety screen, or minimum expected cost when costs are known. Re-check calibration first; a miscalibrated model makes the threshold meaningless when prevalence shifts. Keep the threshold outside the model so it can be tuned without retraining.

questions.q: What is calibration and how do you measure and fix it?
questions.a: A calibrated model's predicted probability matches the observed frequency: among predictions of 0.8, about 80% are positive. Measure it with a reliability diagram and expected calibration error (ECE), or Brier score. Modern neural nets are often over-confident. Fixes: temperature scaling (one scalar fitted on validation logits), Platt scaling, isotonic regression, label smoothing during training, and ensembling. Calibration matters whenever the score drives a threshold, a ranking across models, or a user-facing confidence.

questions.q: Explain cross-validation and when k-fold is the wrong tool.
questions.a: k-fold trains k models on k-1 folds and evaluates on the held-out fold to estimate generalization with less variance than a single split. It is wrong when rows are not exchangeable: time series need forward-chaining splits, grouped data (many rows per user or device) need GroupKFold so a group never spans train and test, and very large datasets make a single held-out set cheaper and sufficient. Also remember that nested CV is required if you use CV both to select hyperparameters and to report the final estimate.

questions.q: Adam vs SGD with momentum: when would you choose each?
questions.a: Adam adapts per-parameter learning rates from running estimates of the first and second gradient moments, so it is forgiving of learning-rate choice and works well for transformers, sparse gradients and embeddings. SGD with momentum often generalizes slightly better for convolutional vision models and is easier to reason about, but needs a tuned schedule. In practice: AdamW with warm-up and cosine decay for transformers; SGD + momentum with step or cosine decay for ResNet-style training; and for fine-tuning use a small learning rate either way.

questions.q: How do you handle missing values?
questions.a: First find out why they are missing (at random, or because of the process: a sensor off, a field only shown to some users), because the mechanism decides the fix. Options: drop rows or columns when rare and uninformative; impute with mean/median/mode or a model; add a missingness indicator feature, which often carries signal; for tree models let the library route missing values natively; for sequences use masking. Never impute using statistics computed on the test set, and check that missingness in production matches training.

questions.q: When does gradient boosting beat a neural network on tabular data, and why?
questions.a: Usually on small to medium tabular datasets with heterogeneous features: trees handle mixed scales, missing values and non-monotonic interactions without feature engineering, train in minutes, and are hard to beat on accuracy below roughly a million rows. Neural nets win when there is a lot of data, when inputs are raw signals (images, audio, text) or when you need embeddings shared across tasks. On device, a boosted model with a few hundred shallow trees is also tiny and runs in microseconds, which is why many Apple ranking and classification features still use them.

questions.q: Explain k-means and its failure modes.
questions.a: Initialize k centroids, assign each point to the nearest centroid, recompute centroids as cluster means, repeat until assignments stop changing. It minimizes within-cluster squared distance and always converges, but to a local optimum, so initialization matters (k-means++ picks spread-out seeds). It assumes spherical, similar-size clusters and is sensitive to outliers and feature scale. Choosing k uses the elbow of inertia or silhouette score. For non-spherical clusters use GMMs or DBSCAN; for huge data use mini-batch k-means.

questions.q: How does PCA work and when would you use it?
questions.a: Center the data, compute the covariance matrix, and take its top eigenvectors: these are orthogonal directions of maximum variance, and projecting onto the first d of them gives the best rank-d reconstruction in squared error. Equivalent to the SVD of the centered data matrix. Use it to decorrelate and reduce dimensions before clustering or linear models, for visualization, and for compressing embeddings. It is linear and variance-based, so it can discard low-variance but predictive directions; scale features first, and never fit it on test data.

questions.q: Random forest vs gradient boosting: what is the core difference?
questions.a: A random forest averages many deep trees trained independently on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, so it reduces variance and is nearly impossible to overfit by adding trees. Gradient boosting trains shallow trees sequentially, each fitting the residual (negative gradient) of the ensemble so far, so it reduces bias and usually reaches higher accuracy but needs tuning of learning rate, depth and number of rounds and can overfit. Forests parallelize trivially; boosting is sequential but each tree is small.

questions.q: Explain the EM algorithm for a Gaussian mixture.
questions.a: Treat the cluster membership of each point as a hidden variable. E-step: with current means, covariances and mixing weights, compute each point's responsibility (posterior probability) for each component. M-step: update each component's weight, mean and covariance as responsibility-weighted statistics. Each iteration does not decrease the log-likelihood, and it converges to a local optimum. k-means is the limit of EM with hard assignments and identical spherical covariances.

questions.q: What is the curse of dimensionality and how does it affect k-NN?
questions.a: As dimensions grow, volume concentrates near the surface of regions and pairwise distances become nearly identical, so 'nearest' loses meaning and the data needed to cover the space grows exponentially. k-NN suffers directly: neighbours are no closer than random points, and the search is expensive. Mitigations: learn a lower-dimensional embedding first (PCA, autoencoder, a metric-learning model), use approximate nearest neighbour indexes, and prefer models with inductive bias.

questions.q: Walk through backpropagation for a two-layer MLP.
questions.a: Forward: z1 = W1 x + b1, h = relu(z1), z2 = W2 h + b2, loss L(z2, y). Backward: dL/dz2 from the loss (for softmax cross-entropy it is p - y); dL/dW2 = dL/dz2 h^T, dL/db2 = dL/dz2; dL/dh = W2^T dL/dz2; dL/dz1 = dL/dh elementwise-times relu'(z1); dL/dW1 = dL/dz1 x^T, dL/db1 = dL/dz1. Each step reuses the forward activations, which is why they are cached and why memory grows with depth and batch size.

questions.q: What does batch normalization do at training time versus inference time?
questions.a: At training time it normalizes each channel using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift; this stabilizes activations and allows higher learning rates. It also keeps running averages of those statistics. At inference it uses the running averages, so the output of a sample no longer depends on its batch, and the whole operation can be folded into the preceding linear layer, which is what on-device compilers do. It degrades with tiny batches, which is one reason transformers use layer norm.

questions.q: Explain self-attention and its complexity.
questions.a: Each token produces a query, key and value vector via learned projections. Attention weights are softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)), row by row, and the output is those weights times V, so every token's representation is a data-dependent mix of all tokens. Multi-head attention runs h such attentions on sliced dimensions and concatenates. Cost is O(n^2 d) time and O(n^2) memory in sequence length, which drives long-context work (flash attention computes it blockwise without materializing the matrix, linear attention approximates it). The sqrt(d_k) keeps logits from growing with dimension so softmax does not saturate.

questions.q: Why do we use residual connections and layer norm in deep networks?
questions.a: Residual connections let each block learn a perturbation of the identity, so gradients flow through the skip path unchanged and very deep networks become trainable; they also make the loss landscape smoother. Layer norm normalizes across features of each token independently of batch, giving stable activation scales for any batch size and sequence length. Pre-norm (norm before the sublayer) trains more stably than post-norm for large transformers; RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction for speed.

questions.q: How do depthwise separable convolutions reduce cost, and what is the catch?
questions.a: A standard conv with k x k kernels from C_in to C_out channels costs k^2 C_in C_out per output position. Splitting it into a depthwise k x k conv per channel (k^2 C_in) followed by a 1x1 pointwise conv (C_in C_out) costs roughly 8-9 times less for 3x3 kernels. The catch: lower arithmetic intensity, so on GPUs and the Neural Engine the speed-up is smaller than the FLOP reduction, and representational capacity per layer drops, so MobileNet-style nets are deeper and use inverted residual blocks to compensate.

questions.q: Explain knowledge distillation and when you would use it.
questions.a: Train a small student to match a large teacher's outputs, usually the softened probabilities (logits divided by a temperature) plus the true labels. The soft targets carry information about similarity between classes that hard labels do not, so the student generalizes better than training on labels alone. Use it to fit a model into an on-device budget, to compress an ensemble into one model, or to transfer from a server model to a smaller one for a specific task. Variants distil intermediate features or attention maps, and sequence-level distillation is used for speech and translation.

questions.q: Your training loss is decreasing but validation loss starts rising after a few epochs. What do you do?
questions.a: That is over-fitting. In order of cost: early stopping on validation loss, stronger regularization (weight decay, dropout), data augmentation, a smaller or pre-trained model, more data or label cleaning. Also check that the validation set is representative and not leaking into training, and that the rise is not just noisy (use a few seeds). If validation accuracy keeps improving while loss rises, the model is becoming over-confident, which is a calibration issue rather than a generalization failure.

questions.q: What is mixed-precision training and why does it need loss scaling?
questions.a: Compute forward and backward in fp16 or bf16 for speed and memory while keeping an fp32 master copy of weights for the update. fp16 has a narrow exponent range, so small gradients underflow to zero; multiplying the loss by a scale factor before backward and dividing the gradients after restores them, with dynamic scaling that backs off on overflow. bf16 has the fp32 exponent range and usually does not need scaling, which is why it is the default on recent hardware.

questions.q: Explain LoRA and why Apple ships adapters rather than separate models.
questions.a: LoRA freezes the base weights and learns a low-rank update W + BA, where B and A are small matrices, for selected layers. Trainable parameters drop by orders of magnitude, optimizer memory shrinks accordingly, and the adapter for a task is a few megabytes. That lets one on-device foundation model serve many features (summarization, tone rewriting, notification priority) by swapping adapters at runtime, which is far cheaper in storage and memory than one model per feature. Adapters can also be merged into the weights for zero inference overhead.

questions.q: How would you evaluate a summarization feature before shipping it?
questions.a: Automatic metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) only for regression testing; they do not track quality well. Build a rubric (faithfulness, coverage, concision, tone) and collect human ratings on a stratified sample of real-like inputs, including adversarial ones. Use an LLM judge only after validating its agreement with humans on that rubric. Measure hallucination rate explicitly with entailment checks against the source. Add safety and privacy tests (PII leakage, refusal behaviour). Then run an online test on satisfaction or edit rate, with the automatic metrics as guardrails.

questions.q: What is RLHF and what does DPO change?
questions.a: RLHF fine-tunes a model with supervised examples, trains a reward model on human preference pairs, then optimizes the policy with PPO against that reward with a KL penalty to the reference model. DPO removes the reward model and RL loop by deriving a closed-form objective on preference pairs that directly increases the log-ratio of the preferred over the rejected response relative to the reference. It is simpler and more stable, at the cost of being offline and tied to the collected pairs. Both are vulnerable to preference data quality and reward hacking.

questions.q: Explain the KV cache and speculative decoding.
questions.a: During autoregressive decoding each new token attends to all previous keys and values; caching them means each step computes attention only for the new token, turning O(n^2) per step into O(n), at the cost of memory proportional to layers x heads x sequence length x head dimension. Speculative decoding runs a small draft model to propose several tokens and the big model verifies them in one forward pass, accepting the prefix that matches its own distribution, giving 2-3x latency gains with identical output distribution. Both matter for on-device assistants where latency and memory are the limits.

questions.q: Design the retrieval part of a RAG system over a user's own documents on device.
questions.a: Chunk documents into passages with overlap and metadata; embed with a small on-device encoder; store in a quantized vector index (e.g. product quantization or HNSW within a memory budget); combine with a lexical index for exact matches like names. At query time embed the query, retrieve top-k from both, merge and re-rank with a small cross-encoder, and pass the top passages to the model with source attributions. Evaluate retrieval recall@k on a labelled set separately from generation. Everything stays on device, which is the privacy constraint Apple would expect you to raise unprompted.

questions.q: Why is byte-pair encoding used and what are its downsides?
questions.a: BPE starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, producing a vocabulary that covers common words as single tokens and rare words as subwords, with no out-of-vocabulary failures. Downsides: token counts vary across languages (some languages cost 3-5x more tokens), numbers and code tokenize awkwardly, the vocabulary is frozen so new domains fragment into many tokens, and tokenization boundaries leak into model behaviour (e.g. trailing-space sensitivity).

questions.q: How much memory does a 3-billion-parameter model need at fp16, int8 and 4-bit, and what else uses memory at inference?
questions.a: Weights alone: about 6 GB at fp16, 3 GB at int8, 1.5 GB at 4-bit (plus small per-group scale factors). Beyond weights: the KV cache (layers x 2 x sequence length x hidden size x bytes, which at long context can rival the weights), activations for the current token, and the runtime's workspace. On an iPhone with a few GB available to an app this is why Apple's on-device model is around 3B parameters with low-bit palettized weights and a bounded context.

questions.q: Post-training quantization made the model noticeably worse. What do you try?
questions.a: First find where the error comes from: compare layer outputs against fp32 to locate sensitive layers, often the first and last layers, attention softmax inputs and layers with outlier channels. Then: per-channel instead of per-tensor scales, keep sensitive layers at higher precision (mixed precision), calibrate scales on representative data instead of min-max, use weight-only quantization with activations in fp16, apply smoothing techniques that move activation outliers into weights, and if still short, quantization-aware training for a few epochs. Measure on the real task metric, not just weight error.

questions.q: Pruning, quantization, distillation: how do you decide which to use?
questions.a: Quantization is the first lever: it cuts memory and often latency with little accuracy loss and no architecture change. Structured pruning (removing whole channels or heads) gives real speed-ups on mobile hardware; unstructured sparsity rarely does without special kernels. Distillation is the most expensive, since it requires retraining, but it can change the architecture entirely to something the Neural Engine runs well and typically gives the best accuracy at a fixed budget. In practice: distil to a mobile-friendly architecture, then prune lightly, then quantize, measuring latency on the oldest target device after each step.

questions.q: Why might a model run slower on the Neural Engine than expected?
questions.a: Unsupported operations force a fallback to GPU or CPU with a copy of tensors across compute units at each boundary; dynamic shapes prevent ahead-of-time compilation; large or unusual tensor layouts, custom ops, and some normalization or gather patterns are not accelerated; and the first inference pays a compilation cost. Diagnose with the performance report in Xcode/Core ML tools to see which ops ran where, then rewrite the graph: fuse ops, fix shapes, replace unsupported layers, and keep precision at fp16 where the engine is fastest.

questions.q: How do you benchmark an on-device model properly?
questions.a: Measure on physical devices, including the oldest supported one, not the simulator. Warm up, then report p50 and p99 latency over many runs, peak memory, and energy or battery impact over a realistic session, under thermal conditions that match use (sustained load throttles). Fix the input distribution to real data shapes. Track model load time separately from inference. Automate it in CI on a device farm so regressions are caught per commit, and set budgets per metric that block a release.

questions.q: How do you ship a model update to an app without a server round-trip for inference?
questions.a: Bundle the model with the app (versioned with the app release) or download it on demand with background assets and verify its signature. Keep a compatibility contract: feature names and shapes, preprocessing version, and a fallback to the previous model if the new one fails a startup self-test. Roll out by cohort using the app's feature flags, compare on-device metrics aggregated with privacy-preserving telemetry, and keep the threshold or calibration parameters separate so they can be tuned without a new model.

questions.q: Define differential privacy and give the intuition.
questions.a: A randomized algorithm is epsilon-differentially private if for any two datasets differing in one person's record, the probability of any output changes by at most a factor of e^epsilon. Intuition: what the algorithm reveals barely depends on whether you are in the data, so an attacker learns almost nothing specific to you. It is achieved by adding calibrated noise (Laplace or Gaussian) scaled to the sensitivity of the query, and it composes: every query spends budget. Local DP adds noise on the device before anything is sent, which is what Apple uses for emoji and keyboard statistics.

questions.q: Explain federated learning and its main practical problems.
questions.a: Devices train on their local data and send only model updates; the server averages them (FedAvg) into a global model and sends it back. Problems: non-IID data across users makes averaging biased and slows convergence; communication is the bottleneck, so updates are compressed and only sampled devices participate per round; devices are unreliable and heterogeneous; updates can still leak information, so secure aggregation and differential privacy are added; and evaluation is hard because you cannot see the data. On iOS it also has to run only while charging and on Wi-Fi.

questions.q: You need to improve a keyboard suggestion model but cannot collect what users type. What do you do?
questions.a: Combine on-device learning with privacy-preserving aggregation: personalize locally so the device adapts to its user without uploading text; use federated learning with secure aggregation and differential privacy to improve the global model from usage signals; collect only local-DP statistics (such as which suggestions were accepted) for evaluation; and train the base model on public and licensed corpora plus synthetic data. Evaluate with on-device A/B tests on aggregate acceptance rate rather than on text samples.

questions.q: How do you size an A/B test to detect a 1% relative lift in a conversion rate of 5%?
questions.a: The absolute lift is 0.05 x 0.01 = 0.0005. Per-group sample size n is about 2 (z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 p(1-p) / delta^2; with alpha 0.05 (1.96) and 80% power (0.84), that is 2 x 7.84 x 0.0475 / 2.5e-7, roughly 3 million users per group. The point to make: small relative lifts on rare events need huge samples, so you reduce variance (CUPED with pre-period covariates), pick a more sensitive proxy metric, or accept a longer test.

questions.q: What is a p-value, and what is the most common mistake made with it?
questions.a: The probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one seen, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and 1 - p is not the probability the effect is real. The common mistakes: peeking at results repeatedly and stopping when p < 0.05 (which inflates false positives unless you use sequential tests), running many metrics without correction, and treating a non-significant result as evidence of no effect when the test was underpowered.

questions.q: Explain the bootstrap and when you would use it.
questions.a: Resample the dataset with replacement many times, recompute the statistic each time, and use the spread of those values as its sampling distribution, giving confidence intervals without a closed form. Use it for metrics with awkward distributions (AUC, medians, ratios, ranking metrics), for small samples, and for comparing two models on the same test set with paired resampling. It assumes the sample represents the population and is expensive for large data, where you can bootstrap on a subsample or use the delta method.

questions.q: A medical test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity for a condition with 0.1% prevalence. What is the probability a positive result is correct?
questions.a: Bayes' rule: P(disease | positive) = 0.99 x 0.001 / (0.99 x 0.001 + 0.01 x 0.999) = 0.00099 / 0.01098, about 9%. Most positives are false because the condition is rare. The same arithmetic applies to any rare-event classifier, which is why health-sensing features need very high specificity and a confirmation step before alerting a user.

questions.q: How do you detect that a deployed model has drifted when labels arrive weeks later?
questions.a: Monitor what you can observe immediately: input feature distributions (population stability index, KL divergence per feature, or a classifier that tries to tell new data from training data), prediction distribution and confidence, and proxy outcomes that correlate with the label (clicks, cancellations). Alert on sustained shifts, not single-day noise, and evaluate by slice. When labels arrive, backfill true metrics and compare with the proxies to recalibrate the alerts. Keep a retraining trigger tied to both drift and label-based degradation.

questions.q: What is your template for an ML system design question?
questions.a: 1) Clarify the product goal, users, constraints (latency, on-device vs server, privacy) and scale. 2) Define success: the online business metric and the offline proxy, plus guardrails. 3) Data: sources, labels and how to get them, volume, freshness, bias. 4) Features and representation. 5) Baseline first (heuristic or simple model), then the model choice with its trade-offs. 6) Training pipeline: splits, validation, hyperparameters, retraining cadence. 7) Serving: where it runs, batching, caching, latency budget, model size. 8) Monitoring, A/B testing, rollback, failure modes and abuse. Spend the first five minutes on 1-2; most candidates jump to 5.

questions.q: How would you evaluate a ranking model offline and online?
questions.a: Offline: build a labelled or implicitly labelled test set that reflects the serving distribution (watch position bias; use inverse propensity weighting or randomized slots), and report NDCG@k, MRR and recall@k by query segment, plus calibration of the scores if they are combined with other signals. Online: an A/B test on the north-star metric (engagement, conversions) with guardrails (latency, diversity, complaints), using interleaving when traffic is scarce because it is far more sensitive. Compare the offline gain with the online lift to keep the offline metric honest.

questions.q: What is a feature store and when is it worth it?
questions.a: A system that computes, stores and serves features consistently for training (point-in-time correct, batch) and inference (low latency, online), so the same definition is used in both and training-serving skew is avoided. Worth it when several models share features, when features are expensive to compute, or when point-in-time correctness has bitten you. Not worth it for a single on-device model whose features are computed from the input itself at inference time.

questions.q: How do you handle training-serving skew?
questions.a: Make the training and serving code paths share the same feature computation (one library or a feature store), log the exact features served and train on those logs, validate schema and distributions of serving features against training statistics, and run a shadow deployment that compares the new model's predictions on live traffic before switching. Add unit tests for preprocessing with golden inputs, and version everything: preprocessing, model, thresholds.

questions.q: How do you decide between running a model on device or on a server?
questions.a: On device when privacy, offline availability, latency or per-request cost matter and the model fits the memory and energy budget on the oldest supported hardware. Server when the model is too large, needs fresh global data, changes often, or benefits from batching and accelerators. Hybrid is common: a small on-device model handles most cases and decides when to escalate, which is the pattern behind Apple's on-device model plus Private Cloud Compute. State the decision criteria explicitly in the design round; interviewers want to hear the trade-off, not a preference.

questions.q: Tell me about a model that failed in production.
questions.a: Use STAR with numbers. Situation: what the model did and its baseline metric. Task: what you owned. Action: how you detected the failure (monitoring, user reports), diagnosed it (drift, a pipeline bug, a label change), and fixed it (rollback, retraining, a new guardrail). Result: the metric after, and the process change that prevents a repeat. Interviewers are listening for ownership, a real root cause rather than 'the data changed', and what you built so it cannot happen silently again.

questions.q: Describe a trade-off you made between model quality and a constraint such as latency, memory or privacy.
questions.a: Pick a case where you quantified both sides: for example, accepting 0.4 points of accuracy loss for a 4x smaller model that fit the on-device budget, with the measurement that justified it and the alternative you rejected. Explain how you set the budget with partners (hardware, design), how you measured on real devices, and what you did to claw back quality (distillation, better data). Apple interviewers like hearing that the user experience, not the leaderboard, decided it.

questions.q: Walk me through your most significant ML project end to end.
questions.a: Two minutes, then let them steer. Cover: the product problem and why ML; data and labels, including what was wrong with them; the baseline and the model that won, with the metric delta; the hardest technical problem and how you solved it; how it shipped and was monitored; what you would do differently. Have the pipeline drawn in your head so you can sketch it, and know the numbers (dataset size, model size, latency, metric lift) without hesitation.

questions.q: How do you work with hardware, design or privacy teams who constrain what the model can do?
questions.a: Describe starting from their constraints as requirements rather than obstacles: get the budget in numbers early (milliseconds, megabytes, what data can be used), build the measurement so everyone sees the same dashboard, prototype inside the constraint before asking for more, and bring options with trade-offs rather than a single ask. Give an example where a constraint made the final product better, which is a story Apple interviewers recognize.

design.title: Notification priority on device
design.prompt: Design the model that decides which notifications to surface immediately versus batch in a summary, running entirely on the user's phone.
outline: Goal and metric: fewer interruptions without missed important messages; online metric is the rate users pull a batched notification forward (a miss) and engagement with surfaced ones; guardrails on battery and latency per notification.

Data: everything stays on device. Labels come from implicit feedback (opened within a minute, dismissed, pulled from summary). Cold start uses a global model trained on opt-in data with local differential privacy or synthetic data.

Features: app, sender relationship signals (contacts, reply frequency), time of day, device state (focus mode, in a meeting), content signals from an on-device text encoder, never raw text leaving the device.
Model: a small gradient-boosted or logistic model over those features with a per-user online-learned layer; a tiny text classifier for urgency. Budget: under a few milliseconds and a few MB.
Serving: run in the notification pipeline with a strict timeout and a safe default (surface) when uncertain; thresholds tunable by focus mode.
Evaluation: on-device A/B via feature flags with privacy-preserving aggregate telemetry; offline replay on opt-in data; slice by app category and locale.

Failure modes: missing a genuinely urgent message (asymmetric cost, so bias toward surfacing), feedback loops where batched notifications get fewer opens, and adversarial senders. Explain the escalation to a server model and why you would avoid it.

design.title: Photo search by natural language
design.prompt: Design search over a user's photo library with free-text queries like 'Maya at the beach last summer', without sending photos to a server.
outline: Goal: recall-oriented retrieval with a precision-ranked top screen; latency under a second on device over tens of thousands of photos.
Representation: a CLIP-style dual encoder distilled to mobile size; image embeddings computed in the background when charging and stored in a quantized index; text encoder runs at query time.

Structured signals: on-device people recognition, places, dates, scene labels; parse the query into entities (person, place, time) plus a free-text residual to combine lexical filters with embedding similarity.
Index: quantized vectors with an approximate nearest neighbour structure sized to the memory budget; incremental updates as photos arrive.
Ranking: fuse embedding similarity, metadata matches and recency with a small learned ranker trained on opt-in or synthetic query logs; re-rank the top 100.
Evaluation: offline recall@k on a labelled benchmark of query-photo pairs across languages; online metric is taps on results and query reformulation rate.

Hard parts to raise: multilingual queries, personal names the text encoder has never seen (route through people recognition), bias in the encoder, and background compute scheduling to protect battery.

design.title: Fall detection on a watch
design.prompt: Design the on-device system that detects a hard fall from accelerometer and gyroscope data and triggers an emergency flow.
outline: Goal and costs: false alarms are annoying and erode trust; misses are dangerous. Set targets per user group (older users first) and define the escalation flow: alert, countdown, call.

Data: lab-collected falls with mannequins and volunteers, plus real-world opt-in data and negatives from daily activity; label with video ground truth; augment with sensor noise and orientation changes.

Features and model: windowed IMU signals, a small 1-D CNN or GRU on device, or hand-engineered impact and stillness features into a boosted model; two-stage design with a cheap always-on trigger and a heavier confirmation model.
Constraints: microwatt budget for the always-on stage, strict latency after impact, run on the watch's sensor coprocessor.
Evaluation: sensitivity and specificity by activity type and age group, false alarms per user-week as the key metric, held-out subjects (group split) to avoid leakage.
Deployment: staged rollout, on-device A/B on alarm rates, post-alert feedback ('I'm OK') as a label source with consent, regulatory documentation.
Follow-ups the interviewer will push on: how you get enough real falls, how you avoid learning the lab, and how you decide the countdown length.

design.title: App Store search ranking
design.prompt: Design the ranking system for App Store search, including how you would evaluate and iterate on it.
outline: Goal: relevant apps that users install and keep; metric is downloads weighted by retention, with guardrails on diversity, fairness to small developers and policy compliance.

Architecture: query understanding (spelling, intent, locale) -> candidate retrieval (lexical index plus two-tower embeddings) -> ranking model (gradient-boosted or neural ranker on hundreds of features) -> business and policy re-ranking.
Features: query-app text match, app quality signals (ratings, crashes, retention), popularity with time decay, personalization from device and prior installs, position-debiased click signals.
Training: implicit labels from installs with position bias correction, point-in-time features from a feature store, daily retraining, offline NDCG@k by locale and query frequency bucket.
Serving: sub-100 ms budget, caching for head queries, feature freshness tiers.
Experimentation: interleaving for sensitivity, then A/B tests on downloads and retention, with long-term holdouts to catch metric gaming.
Failure modes: popularity feedback loops, keyword stuffing by developers, cold-start apps, and regional fairness; describe a mitigation for each.

plan.title: Fundamentals and coding baseline
items: Read and reproduce from memory: bias-variance, regularization, loss functions, metrics, validation (the ML fundamentals topic).
Derive logistic regression and softmax gradients by hand; implement them in the ML Coding problems.
Daily: 2 problems from the Apple track (arrays, strings, linked lists), timed.
Write one-page summaries of your two deepest projects with numbers.

plan.title: Classical ML, statistics and metrics code
items: Classical ML topic: trees and boosting, k-means, PCA, EM. Explain each aloud in two minutes.
Statistics: A/B sizing, p-values, Bayes' rule problems; do the sample-size calculation by hand.
Implement the metrics and unsupervised routines in the ML Coding set.
Daily: 2 Apple-track problems, now including trees and design.

plan.title: Deep learning, LLMs and on-device
items: Deep learning topic: backprop by hand, normalization, attention, CNN cost accounting.
On-device topic: memory arithmetic for quantized models, distillation vs pruning vs quantization, Core ML compute units.
NLP topic: LoRA, RLHF/DPO, KV cache, RAG; answer the question bank for these categories from memory.
Implement attention and batch norm from scratch; time yourself at 25 minutes each.

plan.title: System design, privacy and mocks
items: Work each of the four design prompts to a full whiteboard answer in 35 minutes, then compare with the outline.
Privacy topic: DP definition, FedAvg, the keyboard question; be able to raise privacy unprompted in any design.
Two full mocks: a coding plus ML-fundamentals round, and a design plus past-work round. Record yourself.
Final pass on the question bank: cover each category until you can answer every question in under two minutes.
